forbidden_conclusions: Managerial and supervisory staff drawing high salary are workmen under IDA

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — SRA Section 10 vs Section 20A Infrastructure Bar
test_cases.query_description: A contractor files a civil suit seeking specific performance of a concession agreement for constructing a national highway expansion and requests an interim injunction restraining the highway authority from terminating the contract. Can the civil court grant an injunction?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: While Section 10 provides for specific performance of contracts, Section 20A (inserted by the 2018 Amendment) creates a mandatory statutory bar prohibiting any court from granting an injunction in suits relating to infrastructure projects specified in the Schedule where the injunction would cause impediment or delay in the progress of the project.
forbidden_conclusions: An interim injunction restraining work on an infrastructure project may be granted routinely under Section 10.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Hindu Succession Daughter's Coparcenary vs Pre-2004 Partition Proviso
test_cases.query_description: A Hindu daughter claims a 1/3rd coparcenary share in ancestral joint family property where a registered partition deed had been executed among her father and brothers on 15 November 2003. Does the 2005 Amendment to Section 6 HSA allow her to reopen this partition?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under the proviso to Section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended by Act 39 of 2005), nothing in sub-section (1) affects or invalidates any disposition or alienation, including any partition, that took place before 20 December 2004. As confirmed by the Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma (2020), registered partitions executed prior to 20 December 2004 are saved and cannot be reopened.
expected_precedent_cites: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1
forbidden_conclusions: Registered partitions executed before 20 December 2004 are automatically invalidated by the 2005 amendment.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Commercial Courts Section 12A Mediation vs Urgent Interim Relief
test_cases.query_description: In a commercial dispute valued at INR 2 Crores with no prayer for urgent interim relief, plaintiff instituted a commercial suit directly in court without exploring pre-institution mediation. Is the suit maintainable or subject to rejection?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under Section 12A(1) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, exhaustion of pre-institution mediation is mandatory for suits not contemplating urgent interim relief. The Supreme Court in Patil Automation (2022) held that suits instituted without complying with Section 12A where no urgent interim relief is claimed are liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
expected_precedent_cites: Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (2022) 10 SCC 1
forbidden_conclusions: Section 12A pre-institution mediation is directory and non-compliance can be cured later without rejecting the plaint.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — IBC Section 32A Clean Slate vs Promoter Criminal Liability
test_cases.query_description: A resolution plan for an insolvent company was approved by NCLT under Section 31 IBC. An economic offences probe had been pending against the company and its erstwhile managing director. Does Section 32A immunize the erstwhile director from criminal prosecution?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 Section 32A(1) Proviso
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: While Section 32A(1) of the IBC extinguishes the criminal liability of the corporate debtor upon approval of a resolution plan and change in management, the proviso to Section 32A(1) explicitly states that every person who was a designated partner, promoter, or officer in default shall continue to be liable to be prosecuted and punished for offences committed prior to CIRP.
expected_precedent_cites: Manish Kumar v. Union of India (2021) 5 SCC 1
Ajay Kumar Radheyshyam Goenka v. Tourism Finance Corp (2023) 4 SCC 320
forbidden_conclusions: Section 32A grants complete criminal immunity to former promoters and directors of the corporate debtor.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — NI Act Section 138 Notice Prerequisite to Section 142 Complaint
test_cases.query_description: A cheque of INR 5 Lakhs was dishonoured on 10 January 2024. The payee issued a demand notice after 45 days on 25 February 2024 and then filed a complaint under Section 138. Is the complaint legally maintainable?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Section 138 Proviso (b) & Section 142
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under proviso (b) to Section 138 of the NI Act, the payee must give notice in writing demanding payment within 30 days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding dishonour. Issuing notice after 45 days fails the statutory condition precedent, and no valid cause of action arises under Section 142.
expected_precedent_cites: K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan (1999) 7 SCC 510
forbidden_conclusions: A statutory demand notice issued after 45 days satisfies Section 138 proviso (b).

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Partial Answer — Active Substantive Law vs Uncommenced Labour Code
test_cases.query_description: Can an employee claim retrenchment compensation under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and can the employer implement new retrenchment thresholds under the uncommenced Industrial Relations Code, 2020?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 Section 25F (In force) vs IR Code 2020 (Uncommenced)
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: This multi-issue inquiry is resolved with calibrated separation: (1) The employee is entitled to retrenchment compensation under Section 25F of the active Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; (2) The employer cannot implement thresholds from the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 because the Central Government has not notified its commencement in the Official Gazette.
forbidden_conclusions: The Industrial Relations Code 2020 has repealed the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Section 53A TPA vs Mandatory Registration Section 17(1A)
test_cases.query_description: A purchaser took possession of an immovable property in 2015 under an unregistered agreement to sell and paid the entire sale consideration. Can they defend possession against the vendor under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Transfer of Property Act Section 53A read with Registration Act Section 17(1A)
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: By Act 48 of 2001 (effective 24 September 2001), Section 17(1A) was inserted into the Registration Act, 1908 and Section 53A of the TPA was amended. Contracts to transfer immovable property for consideration for the purposes of Section 53A must be registered; if unregistered, they have no effect for the purposes of Section 53A.
expected_precedent_cites: Ameer Minhaj v. Dierdre Elizabeth (Wright) Issac (2018) 7 SCC 639
forbidden_conclusions: An unregistered agreement to sell executed after 2001 provides valid protection of possession under Section 53A TPA.

test_cases.domain: Cross-Statute Non-Obstante Priority — IBC Section 238 vs Electricity/Customs Claims
test_cases.query_description: During corporate insolvency resolution under IBC, a state electricity distribution company claims priority of its arrears over financial creditors citing its statutory charge under state electricity regulations. Does the IBC waterfall prevail?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 Section 238 & Section 53
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of the Code have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law for the time being in force. Per Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam (2023) and Sundaresh Bhatt (2022), government and statutory dues are subordinated to the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 IBC.
expected_precedent_cites: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Pvt. Ltd. (2023) 10 SCC 60
Sundaresh Bhatt v. CBIC (2022) 10 SCC 700
forbidden_conclusions: State electricity regulation charges take precedence over Section 53 IBC waterfall distribution.

test_cases.domain: Coordinate High Court Conflict — Arbitral Mandate Extension Without Territorial Jurisdiction
test_cases.query_description: Can a court extend the mandate of an arbitral tribunal under Section 29A of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act after the statutory 18-month period has expired, or is the tribunal's mandate automatically terminated?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Coordinate High Courts have delivered conflicting rulings on whether Section 29A applications can be filed after mandate expiry (e.g., Delhi High Court in Harkirat vs Bombay High Court in Rohan Builders, pending larger bench resolution). Territorial High Court jurisdiction is required to resolve binding authority.
expected_precedent_cites: Rohan Builders (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Berger Paints India Ltd.
forbidden_conclusions: One High Court's interpretation of Section 29A is nationally binding without specifying territorial jurisdiction.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Copyright Fair Dealing Section 52 vs Moral Rights Section 57
test_cases.query_description: An academic institution reproduces portions of an author's architectural sketches for non-commercial educational instruction. The author claims violation of moral rights under Section 57 because their name was omitted. Does Section 52 fair dealing defend against moral rights claims?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: While Section 52(1)(a) provides statutory exceptions for fair dealing in educational and research contexts, Section 57 confers special, perpetual moral rights (paternity and integrity) that exist independently of copyright and are not extinguished by fair dealing exceptions.
expected_precedent_cites: Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India (2005) 30 PTC 253 (Del)
forbidden_conclusions: Section 52 fair dealing permits complete omission of author attribution without moral rights liability.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Patent Therapeutic Efficacy Section 3(d) vs Form 27 Rules
test_cases.query_description: An applicant claims a patent on an incremental derivative of a known pharmaceutical substance and submits working statements under Form 27 of Patent Rules, 2003. Does procedural compliance with Form 27 satisfy the substantive therapeutic efficacy requirement under Section 3(d)?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Patents Act, 1970 Section 3(d) read with Patent Rules, 2003 Form 27
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Compliance with delegated procedural rules (Form 27 working statements) does not displace substantive patentability criteria under Section 3(d). Per Novartis (2013), incremental modifications require proof of significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
expected_precedent_cites: Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013) 6 SCC 1
forbidden_conclusions: Filing Form 27 creates a statutory presumption that Section 3(d) therapeutic efficacy is established.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Partial Answer — Cheque Dishonour Cause of Action vs Condonation of Delay
test_cases.query_description: A payee served a 15-day notice under Section 138 NI Act on time, but due to medical hospitalization filed the criminal complaint after 45 days. Is the delay condonable under Section 142(1)(b) proviso?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under the proviso to Section 142(1)(b) of the NI Act (inserted by Act 55 of 2002), the court may take cognizance of a complaint after the prescribed 1-month period if the complainant satisfies the court that they had sufficient cause for not making the complaint within such period.
expected_precedent_cites: MSR Leathers v. S. Palaniappan (2013) 1 SCC 177
forbidden_conclusions: The 1-month limitation under Section 142(1)(b) is absolute and can never be condoned under any circumstances.

test_cases.domain: Downstream Claim Dependency — Prerequisite Failure Article 54 Limitation
test_cases.query_description: A purchaser seeks specific performance under Section 10 SRA for an agreement to sell where the fixed completion date was 1 January 2018, and the suit was instituted on 15 March 2024 without any extension. Can specific performance be decreed?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Specific Relief Act Section 10 barred by Article 54 Limitation Act, 1963
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for a suit for specific performance is three years from the date fixed for performance. Instituting the suit after six years without an extension extinguishes the remedy, so the downstream claim for specific performance under Section 10 cannot succeed.
forbidden_conclusions: Specific performance can be decreed under Section 10 SRA regardless of the 3-year limitation under Article 54.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Commercial Court Mediation Exemption for Urgent Injunction
test_cases.query_description: A plaintiff in a commercial trademark infringement suit seeks an ex-parte ad-interim injunction to prevent imminent dispatch of infringing goods. Must they exhaust Section 12A mediation before approaching the Commercial Court?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Commercial Courts Act, 2015 Section 12A(1) Urgent Relief Exemption
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under Section 12A(1) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, the requirement of exhausting pre-institution mediation applies only to a suit 'which does not contemplate any urgent interim relief'. Where urgent interim relief (such as an ex-parte injunction against infringing goods) is sought, the suit may be instituted directly without prior mediation.
expected_precedent_cites: Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (2022) 10 SCC 1
forbidden_conclusions: All commercial suits, even those seeking urgent ex-parte interim injunctions, must undergo 3 months of mediation first.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — Hindu Succession Coparcenary Alienation Prior to Cutoff
test_cases.query_description: Ancestral agricultural lands of a Hindu family were sold by registered sale deed on 10 August 2004 by the father and sons. Can an unmarried daughter challenge this sale in 2024 claiming coparcenary rights under Section 6 HSA?
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Under the proviso to Section 6(1) HSA, dispositions and alienations that took place prior to 20 December 2004 are preserved and cannot be invalidated or reopened on the basis of daughter's newly conferred coparcenary status.
expected_precedent_cites: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1
forbidden_conclusions: All alienations of coparcenary property made between 1956 and 2004 can be challenged by daughters under amended Section 6.

test_cases.domain: Multi-Issue Synthesis — SRA Section 20A Sub-Contractor Injunction Impediment
test_cases.query_description: A sub-contractor for a metro rail construction project seeks an interim mandatory injunction against the main contractor for release of withheld payment and staying appointment of replacement contractors. Does Section 20A SRA apply?
test_cases.expected_governing_regime: Specific Relief Act Section 20A read with Schedule (Transport Sub-Sector)
test_cases.expected_disentangled_rationale: Metro rail projects are specified infrastructure projects under the Schedule to the Specific Relief Act. Under Section 20A, courts are barred from granting any injunction that causes impediment or delay in the progress of the infrastructure project.

test_cases.domain: Cross-Domain Interplay — IBC Section 32A Clean Slate vs Money Laundering Attachments
